subject: Career
title: Addressing the Hiring Manager by Name
description: A 60-second lesson on Addressing the Hiring Manager by Name.

hook.text: 'Dear Hiring Manager' is the cover letter equivalent of 'To Whom It May Concern.'

buildup.text: Finding the hiring manager's name signals initiative. LinkedIn and company pages usually reveal it.

discovery.text: Personalization triggers the cocktail party effect — people notice their own name.

twist.text: If you truly can't find a name, address the team: 'Dear Product Team' still beats 'Dear Sir/Madam.'

climax.text: This small effort separates you from the 90% who didn't bother.

punchline.text: Use their name. It's the easiest win in hiring.

quiz.question: Why is addressing the hiring manager by name effective?
options: It signals initiative and triggers personal attention

details.summary: Addressing a cover letter to the specific hiring manager by name demonstrates research effort and creates a personal connection before they even read the content. It signals genuine interest in the company rather than a mass application approach.
details.whyItMatters: A personalized salutation immediately differentiates your letter from the majority that start with 'Dear Hiring Manager' or 'To Whom It May Concern,' signaling higher effort and genuine interest.
takeaways: Research the hiring manager's name through LinkedIn or the company website
If the name is truly unfindable, use a specific team or department address
Avoid outdated salutations like 'Dear Sir or Madam'

faq.question: How do you find the hiring manager's name when it is not listed in the job posting?
faq.answer: Search LinkedIn for the job title one level above the open role at that company. Check the company's about or team page. Look at who posted the job on the company's social accounts. If all else fails, call the front desk. Even five minutes of research shows more effort than most applicants invest.

faq.question: Is it better to address the wrong person by name than to use a generic salutation?
faq.answer: No. Addressing the wrong person can appear careless rather than diligent. If you are unsure, use 'Dear Hiring Team' or 'Dear [Department] Team' rather than guessing. A specific but accurate department address is better than an incorrect individual name.
